A B S T R A C T
Recently, the state space model Mamba has demonstrated efficient long-sequence model-
ing capabilities, particularly for addressing long-sequence visual tasks in 3D medical
imaging. However, existing generative self-supervised learning methods have not yet
fully unleashed Mamba’s potential for handling long-range dependencies because they
overlook the inherent causal properties of state space sequences in masked modeling.
To address this challenge, we propose a general-purpose pre-training framework called
MambaMIM, a masked image modeling method based on a novel TOKen-Interpolation
strategy (TOKI) for the selective structure state space sequence, which learns causal rela-
tionships of state space within the masked sequence. Further, MambaMIM introduces a
bottom-up 3D hybrid masking strategy to maintain a masking consistency across differ-
ent architectures and can be used on any single or hybrid Mamba architecture to enhance
its multi-scale and long-range representation capability. We pre-train MambaMIM on a
large-scale dataset of 6.8K CT scans and evaluate its performance across eight public
medical segmentation benchmarks. Extensive downstream experiments reveal the feasi-
bility and advancement of using Mamba for medical image pre-training. In particular,
when we apply the MambaMIM to a customized architecture that hybridizes MedNeXt
and Vision Mamba, we consistently obtain the state-of-the-art segmentation performance.

2. Related Works
In this section, we first introduce the previous masked image
modeling methods. Then, we survey the existing self-supervised
methods in medical image analysis. Finally, we review the
recent Mamba-based methods for medical tasks and discuss the
importance of introducing a self-supervised method for Mamba.
2.1. Masked image modeling
Driven by BERT (Bao et al., 2021), masked image modeling
(MIM) aims to remove or corrupt portions of the visual input
and learn to predict the corrupted ones (Pathak et al., 2016; Xie
et al., 2022b; He et al., 2022; Tian et al., 2023; Assran et al.,
2022b). These approaches have been studied to reveal their
ability to learn local attention patterns (Zhang et al., 2022a) and
demonstrate better transferability to downstream tasks, such as
segmentation and detection (He et al., 2022; Xie et al., 2022b;
Chen et al., 2024; Tian et al., 2023). However, MIM methods
necessitate handling both masked and seen patches, typically
involving strategies tailored to specific architectures (Xie et al.,
2022b; He et al., 2022; Tian et al., 2023). One representative
MIM technique is MAE (He et al., 2022), which pre-trains Vi-
sion Transformer (ViT) (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020) by handling
only a small subset of visible patches. This computationally
efficient approach offers significant advantages for 3D medi-
cal SSL (Li et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2023b). However, these
methods ignore the structural sequence relationships within the
state space, impairing Mamba’s ability to learn effective rep-
resentations. Unlike previous works, MambaMIM emphasizes
the importance of learning causal relationships within the state
space, learning the state space relationships between unmasked
tokens to generate masked tokens for pixel space reconstruction.

2.2. Self-supervised learning for medical image analyses
Due to the scarcity of labeled medical images, self-supervised
learning (SSL) has emerged as a promising approach for medical
image analysis (Li et al., 2023). Existing medical SSL methods
are primarily based on contrastive learning, typically employing
strong data augmentation techniques, such as rotation (Tang
et al., 2022; Tao et al., 2020) and multi-view crops (Zhou et al.,
2023a; Xie et al., 2022a; Wu et al., 2024; He et al., 2023; Gon-
charov et al., 2023; Haghighi et al., 2021). However, most of
these methods learn modality-related high-level semantic repre-
sentations (Assran et al., 2022b), which introduce significant bi-
ases in downstream tasks with different data distributions (Zhang
et al., 2023; Assran et al., 2022a). In contrast, introducing MIM
methods for medical imaging pre-training (Chen et al., 2023;
Zhou et al., 2023b) offers a promising avenue for addressing
these challenges (Li et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023). MIM can
learn robust local patterns (Zhang et al., 2022b), which yield
substantial benefits for various downstream tasks (Li et al., 2023;
Chen et al., 2023), such as medical image segmentation, while
also offering improved generalization ability. However, there is
currently no existing MIM approach specifically designed for
Mamba, which is a promising architecture capable of efficiently
handling long sequences of 3D medical images.
2.3. Mamba in medical image analyses
Long-range dependency modeling is critical for 3D medical
image analysis tasks (Liu et al., 2024b; Bansal et al., 2024). In
recent years, this capability has been enabled by Transform-
ers (Vaswani et al., 2017).
However, Transformers exhibit
quadratic complexity with respect to sequence length, which
can pose a computational challenge for high-resolution 3D med-
ical images (Liu et al., 2024b; Bansal et al., 2024). Recently,
Mamba, with its hybrid architectures, has been introduced for
medical image analysis tasks, such as classification (Nasiri-
Sarvi et al., 2024), reconstruction (Huang et al., 2024a), reg-
istration (Guo et al., 2024), and segmentation (Ma et al., 2024;
Xing et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024a), demonstrating compara-
ble performance to Transformers while significantly reducing
computational overhead. Given the labor-intensive annotations
of medical images (Ma et al., 2021; Luo et al., 2022) and the
importance of efficient long-range dependency modeling in 3D
medical image analysis (Liu et al., 2024b; Bansal et al., 2024),
pre-training Mamba and transferring it for downstream tasks
presents a promising solution for label-efficient learning.
3. Methodology
To solve the problem of pre-training methods for any hy-
brid mamba, we proposed a generative self-supervised learning
method MambaMIM. The overall framework of MambaMIM
is illustrated in Fig. 4, which consists of two components: hier-
archical hybrid encoding (Sec 3.2) and decoding (Sec 3.3) are
used for bottom-up hybrid mask modeling; Selective Structured
State Space Sequence Token-interpolation (Sec 3.4) is used for
learning causal relationships within state space modeling. Aside
from the Vision Mamba baseline, we further propose to use
a CNN-Mamba hybrid model, called HyMamba (CNN on the
top and Vision Mamba at the bottom) as the baseline backbone,
to fully reveal the potential of our proposed MambaMIM and
Mamba structure.
3.1. Baseline models
Vanilla Mamba.
For vanilla Mamba, we utilize the UN-
ETR (Hatamizadeh et al., 2022) network, where the Vision
Transformer (ViT) is replaced by Vision Mamba (Zhu et al.,
2024a). Following the patch embedding practice in UNETR,
we set the patch size of 16 × 16 × 16, depth of 12 and embed-
ding dims of 768, and use the same bottleneck and decoder of
UNETR in vanilla Mamba.
HyMamba. For hybrid Mamba (HyMamba), the encoder adopts
a serial architecture consisting of two stages: the CNN stage and
the Mamba stage. In the CNN stage, we choose MedNeXt (Roy
et al., 2023) (the state-of-the-art ConvNet in medical tasks) as
the top part of the encoder. In the Mamba stage, we implement
the standard Vision Mamba (Zhu et al., 2024a) as the bottom part
of the encoder. It is worth noting that we substitute the downsam-
pling layers of MedNeXt with max-pooling. For downstream
tasks, we utilize the MedNeXt’s decoder for segmentation. we
set hierarchical CNN with 4 stages and the patch size is 16 × 16
× 16 during pre-training, fine-tuning, and testing.

Mamba relies on a state space model (SSM), where each
output depends on previous states in a continuous, structured
manner. However, traditional methods such as MAE (He et al.,
2022) face challenges when applied to Mamba, as they often
fill masked regions with random or learnable tokens, which
disrupts the causal flow of a sequence, making it harder for
state-space models to learn high-quality representations. TOKI
addresses this key challenge in applying MIM to Mamba-based
networks. Unlike traditional methods that insert learnable to-
kens into masked regions, TOKI leverages the inherent causal
relationships within Mamba’s state-space sequences and math-
ematically interpolates the masking state-space token, which
ensures the filled tokens respect the causal flow of the sequence.

4. Experiment
4.1. Dataset
Pre-training datasets. As shown in Table.1, our pre-training
dataset includes 6814 CT scans of various body region of in-
terest (ROI) such as head, neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis.
It is composed of 13 public datasets: BTCV (Landman et al.,
2015), CHAOS (Kavur et al., 2021), WORD (Luo et al., 2022),
FLARE’22 (Ma et al., 2023), AbdomenCT-1k (Ma et al., 2021),
TotalSegmentator (Wasserthal et al., 2023), AMOS (Ji et al.,
2022), and MSD (Antonelli et al., 2022). Existing labels are not
utilized from these datasets during the pre-training stage.
BTCV dataset. The Multi-Atlas Labeling Beyond The Cranial
Vault (BTCV) (Landman et al., 2015) dataset consists of 30
subjects with abdominal CT scans where 13 organs are annotated
at pixel level by interpreters under the supervision of clinical
radiologists at Vanderbilt University Medical Center. Our data
preprocessing strategy is the same as UNETR (Hatamizadeh
et al., 2022).
MSD dataset.
Medical Segmentation Decathlon (MSD)
dataset (Antonelli et al., 2022) comprises of ten segmentation
tasks from different organs and image modalities. We only use
three CT datasets: Pancreas, Hepatic Vessel, Spleen dataset. All
the pre-processing strategy is the same as Swin UNETR (Tang
et al., 2022).
AMOS dataset. The Multi-Modality Abdominal Multi-Organ
Segmentation Challenge (AMOS) dataset (Ji et al., 2022) com-
prises 360 CT and MRI scans annotated for 15 abdominal or-
gans. The data preprocessing strategy is the same as Swin UN-
ETR (Hatamizadeh et al., 2022).
CT-ORG dataset. The CT-ORG dataset (Rister et al., 2020)
consists of 150 CT scans for the five organ and bone annota-
tions from several clinical sites. It is used for multiple organ
segmentation.
KiTS 23 dataset. The 2023 Kidney and Kidney Tumor Segmen-
tation challenge (KiTS 23) dataset (Heller et al., 2023) consists
of 489 CT scans for the Kidney and its Tumor and Cyst annota-
tions from M Health Fairview medical center.
BraTS 21 dataset. The BraTS 21 dataset (Baid et al., 2021),
from the BraTS 2021 challenge of brain tumors by providing
1251 MRI scans with pixel-level annotations. Following the
previous works (Tang et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2024), we utilize
the same dataset split, i.e., with 1000 scans for training and 251
scans for validation, for fair comparison. The data preprocessing
strategy is the same as Swin UNETR (Hatamizadeh et al., 2022).
4.2. Implementation details
Implementation of pre-training. The pre-training data are
interpolated to isotropic voxel spacing of 1.5 mm. Intensities
are scaled to [-175, 250] and then normalized to [0,1]. We crop
sub-volumes of 96 × 96 × 96 voxels. For pre-training tasks, we
train with the AdamW optimizer, a learning rate of 1e-4, and a
cosine-annealing learning rate scheduler. The batch size is set to
8, and the model is trained for 100 epochs on a single GPU.

tion tasks, a five-fold cross-validation strategy is used to train
models for BTCV and MSD experiments, and the best model is

4.3. Results and discussion
Performance of MambaMIM. We first validate the proposed
method MambaMIM and its baseline model on BTCV. The re-
sults are listed in Table 2. Our HyMamba achieves the highest
average metric of 77.56% when trained from scratch, surpass-
ing Mamba by 6.62% (77.56% vs. 70.94%) and SegMamba
by 1.02% (77.56% vs. 76.54%). This shows that the hybrid
architecture can maximize the long-range extraction capability
of Mamba, which is crucial for medical image segmentation
tasks. More importantly, MambaMIM gains a huge leap in
DSC score (2.6% improvement, 80.16% vs 77.56%). For or-
gans that are small in scale and challenging to segment, such as
gallbladder (Gall: 5.26% improvement), stomach (Sto: 6.60%
improvement), pancreas (Pan: 7.58% improvement), etc., the
performance improvements highlight MambaMIM’s capability
to effectively capture both local and global representations.

5. Conclusions
The success of Mamba in vision tasks prompts us to ex-
plore their potential in downstream tasks after being well pre-
trained using large-scale unlabeled medical images. In this paper,
we introduce MambaMIM, a novel generative self-supervised
method based on selective structure state space sequence token-
interpolation for single and hybrid Mamba architectures. Our
method uses a bottom-up masking strategy to guarantee the con-
sistency of masking between CNN and Mamba. Additionally,
TOKI is employed to learn causal relationships between the
masked sequences in the state space. Extensive downstream
and ablation experiments demonstrate the superior performance
of our pre-training method. We believe that MambaMIM can
further benefit our community and our findings can inspire more
work to maximize the potential of Mamba in various visual tasks.
